{{Short description|Concept in combinatorics}}
[[File:Hook-length tableau December 8 2013 3.jpg|thumb|right|A 6-core partition, with the hook length of each cell labelled.]]

In [[Combinatorics|combinatorial mathematics]], a '''{{mvar|t}}-core partition''' is a [[integer partition|partition]] which has no hooks of length {{mvar|t}}. Such partitions have been used in the study of [[Ramanujan's congruences]] on the [[Partition function (number theory)|partition function]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Garvan |first1=Frank |last2=Kim |first2=Dongsu |last3=Stanton |first3=Dennis |title=Cranks and t-cores |journal=Invent. Math. |date=1990 |volume=101 |issue=1 |pages=1–17}}</ref> and for [[representation theory]] of the [[symmetric group]],<ref>{{cite book |last1=James |first1=Gordon |last2=Kerber |first2=Albert |title=The representation theory of the symmetric group |date=1981 |publisher=Addison-Wesley Publishing Co. |location=Reading, Mass.}}</ref> especially [[modular representation theory]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Olsson |first1=Jørn B. |last2=Stanton |first2=Dennis |title=Block inclusions and cores of partitions |journal=Aequationes Math. |date=2007 |volume=74 |issue=1-2 |pages=90–110}}</ref>

== Definition ==

A partition <math>\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)</math> is a weakly decreasing list of positive [[integers]], which we associate with its [[Integer partition#Young diagram|Young diagram]] by drawing <math>\lambda_i</math> square cells in row {{mvar|i}} of an array. The size of a partition, denoted <math>|\lambda|</math>, is the sum of all <math>\lambda_i</math>, or the total number of cells. The [[Integer partition#Conjugate and self-conjugate partitions|conjugate partition]] <math>\lambda'</math> is the partition whose values are the length of each column in <math>\lambda</math>.

The cells in the diagram are labelled by <math>(i,j)</math> for <math>1\leq i\leq k</math> and <math>1\leq j\leq \lambda_i</math>. The ''hook length'' <math>h_\lambda(i,j)</math> of cell <math>(i, j)</math> is given by
<math display="block">h_\lambda(i,j)=\lambda_i+\lambda_j'-i-j+1,</math>
which is equal to the number of cells in the rotated L-shaped hook with vertex at <math>(i,j)</math> which extends to the right and downwards.

For a positive integer {{mvar|t}}, a partition is {{mvar|t}}-core if it has no cells with a hook length of {{mvar|t}}.

== Properties ==

If a partition is {{mvar|t}}-core, then it is also ({{mvar|nt}})-core for every positive integer {{mvar|n}}.

In any row/column of a {{mvar|t}}-core partition which contains a cell of hook length {{mvar|h}} > {{mvar|t}}, there is a cell in the same row/column with hook length {{mvar|h}} – {{mvar|t}}.<ref name="james">{{cite journal |last1=James |first1=Gordon |title=Some combinatorial results involving Young diagrams |journal=Math Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. |date=1978 |volume=83 |issue=1 |pages=1–10}}</ref>

The only {{math|1}}-core partition is the empty partition with no cells. The {{math|2}}-core partitions are the staircase partitions <math>\lambda=(k,\dots,2,1)</math>. If <math>\rho</math> is the [[perimeter]] of the Young diagram of a partition, then this partition is {{mvar|t}}-core for every <math>t\geq\rho/2</math>.

{| class="wikitable" style="float:right;line-spacing:0.8;margin-left:1ex;"
|+ Number of {{mvar|t}}-core partitions of size {{mvar|n}}.
|-
! {{diagonal split header|{{mvar|t}}|{{mvar|n}}}} !! 1 !! 2 !! 3 !! 4 !! 5 !! 6
|-

For every integer {{mvar|t}} at least {{math|4}}, there exists a {{mvar|t}}-core partition of size {{mvar|n}} for every positive integer {{mvar|n}}. This result was known as the ''{{mvar|t}}-core conjecture'' before finally being proven by [[Andrew Granville]] and [[Ken Ono]] in 1996.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Granville |first1=Andrew |last2=Ono |first2=Ken |title=Defect zero p-blocks for finite simple groups |journal=Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. |date=1996 |volume=348 |issue=1 |pages=331–347}}</ref>

If <math>c_t(n)</math> is the number of {{mvar|t}}-core partitions of size {{mvar|n}}, we have the [[generating function]]
<math display="block">\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_t(n)q^n=\frac{\phi\left(q^t\right)^t}{\phi(q)}</math>
where <math>\phi(q)=(1-q) \left(1-q^2\right) \left(1-q^3\right)\cdots</math> is the [[Euler function]]. Note that <math>1/\phi(q)</math> is the generating function for all partitions.

== Abacus ==

The generating function for {{mvar|t}}-core partitions implies that there is a [[bijection]] between partitions <math>\lambda</math> and pairs <math display="inline">\left(\lambda^{(t)},\Lambda_{(t)}\right)</math>, where <math>\lambda^{(t)}</math> is a {{mvar|t}}-core partition and <math display="inline">\Lambda_{(t)}= \left(\lambda_{(1)},\dots,\lambda_{(t-1)}\right)</math> is a sequence of partitions such that
<math display="block">|\lambda|= \left|\lambda^{(t)}\right|+t \left(\left|\lambda_{(0)}\right|+\cdots+\left|\lambda_{(t-1)}\right|\right).</math>
We call <math>\lambda^{(t)}</math> the '''{{mvar|t}}-core''' of <math>\lambda</math> and <math>\Lambda^{(t)}</math> the '''{{mvar|t}}-quotient''' of <math>\lambda</math>.

=== Construction ===

We give a construction of this bijection using an [[abacus]].<ref name="james" /> For a partition <math>\lambda</math>, define the infinite [[Set (mathematics)|set]] <math>\beta^\lambda=\{\lambda_i-i\mid i\geq 1\}</math> where <math>\lambda_i=0</math> for every <math>i>k</math>. Given the set <math>\beta</math>, we can recover <math>\lambda</math> as follows: shift all entries of <math>\beta</math> so that {{math|0}} is the smallest number which doesn't appear. Then the positive entries of this shifted set are the hook lengths of the first column of <math>\lambda</math>.

Consider an abacus with {{mvar|t}} infinitely long vertical runners numbered {{math|0}}, {{math|1}}, up to {{math|''t'' – 1}}. Label the position on runner <math>r</math> at height <math>s</math> by <math>st+r</math>, so values increase left-to-right then bottom-to-top.

Given a partition <math>\lambda</math>, place beads on the abacus at each position in <math>\beta^\lambda</math>. If <math>\beta_{(r)}</math> are the heights of the beads on runner <math>r</math>, then <math>\lambda_{(r)}</math> is the unique partition with <math>\beta^{\lambda_{(r)}}=\beta_{(r)}</math>. Next, suppose <math>\beta'</math> are the positions of the beads when the beads in <math>\beta^\lambda</math> naturally fall under [[gravity]]. Then <math>\lambda^{(t)}</math> is the unique partition satisfying <math>\beta^{\lambda^{(t)}}=\beta'</math>.

=== Example ===

Suppose <math>\lambda=(11,6,6,3,3,2,1,1)</math> and <math>t=4</math>. Then
<math display="block">\beta^\lambda=\{10,4,3,-1,-2,-4,-6,-7,-9,-10,-11,\dots\}</math>

We draw our {{math|4}}-abacus by circling the beads in <math>\beta^\lambda</math>.

[[File:4-abacus with beta set.svg|frameless|center|upright=0.5]]

Looking at runner {{math|0}} (the first column), the shaded beads have heights <math>\beta_{(0)}=\{1,-1,-3,-4,-5,\dots\}</math>. Hence, the first-column hook lengths of <math>\lambda_{(1)}</math> are <math>\{3,1\}</math>, and so <math>\lambda_{(0)}=(2,1).</math>

In runner {{math|1}}, we have <math>\beta_{(1)}=\{-2,-3,\dots\}</math> and so <math>\lambda_{(1)}</math> is the empty partition <math>()</math>. We have <math>\beta_{(2)}=\{2,-1,-2,\dots\}</math> so <math>\lambda_{(2)}=(2)</math>, and finally <math>\lambda_{(3)}=(1,1)</math>. These partitions make up the {{math|4}}-quotient <math>\Lambda^{(4)}</math>.

Now we calculate the {{math|4}}-core of <math>\lambda</math>. Letting the beads of <math>\beta^\lambda</math> fall under gravity gives the abacus:

[[File:4-abacus with beta set after gravity.svg|frameless|center|upright=0.5]]

Therefore,
<math display="block">\beta'=\{2,-1,-2,-4,-5,-6,\dots\}.</math>
The smallest missing value is {{math|–3}}, so shifting the values by {{math|3}} gives the first-column hook lengths <math>\{5,2,1\}</math> which means <math>\lambda^{(4)}=(3,1,1)</math>, which is indeed a {{math|4}}-core partition.

== Other identities ==

Ramanujan's modular equations can be used to prove identities for <math>c_t(n)</math>, such as <math>c_3(4n+1)=c_3(n)</math> and <math>c_5(4n+3)=c_5(2n+1)+2c_5(n)</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Baruah |first1=Nayandeep |last2=Berndt |first2=Bruce |title=Partition identities and Ramanujan's modular equations |journal=J. Combin. Theory Ser. A |date=2007 |volume=114 |issue=6 |pages=1024–1045}}</ref>

Partitions which are simultaneously {{mvar|t}}-core for multiple values of {{mvar|t}} are well-studied.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cho |first1=Hyunsoo |last2=Kim |first2=Byungchan |last3=Nam |first3=Hayan |last4=Sohn |first4=Jaebum |title=A survey on t-core partitions |journal=Hardy-Ramanujan Journal |date=2021 |volume=44 |pages=81–101}}</ref> For example, if {{mvar|s}} and {{mvar|t}} are [[coprime]] positive integers, then the number of partitions which are simultaneously {{mvar|s}}-core and {{mvar|t}}-core is equal to
<math display="block">\frac{1}{s+t}\binom{s+t}{s},</math>
which is a [[Catalan number#Generalizations|rational Catalan number]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Anderson |first1=Jaclyn |title=Partitions which are simultaneously t1- and t2-core |journal=Discrete Math |date=2002 |volume=248 |issue=1-3 |pages=237–243}}</ref>

The number of {{mvar|t}}-core partitions with at most {{mvar|k}} rows is equal to the number of partitions with at most {{mvar|k}} rows and at most {{math|''t'' – 1}} columns. A bijection between these sets is given by <math>\lambda\mapsto \partial</math>, where <math>\partial_i</math> is the number of cells in row <math>i</math> of <math>\lambda</math> whose hook length is less than {{mvar|t}}.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lapointe |first1=Luc |last2=Morse |first2=Jennifer |title=Tableaux on k+1-cores, reduced words for affine permutations, and k-Schur expansions |journal=Journal of Comb. Thy., Series A |date=2005 |volume=112 |issue=1 |pages=44–81}}</ref>
